title: Interchangeable Primitive Parameters with Distinct Domain Meanings
pattern: A function accepts consecutive same-primitive parameters with different semantic roles, or accepts multiple distinct domain identifiers represented by the same integer, UUID, or other underlying primitive type, allowing a semantically swapped call to type-check.
why_bad: The type system checks only the shared representation, not the role, so a caller who swaps values gets a program that compiles yet silently performs the wrong association, corrupts data, or executes invalid logic.
detection: Subcase A: consecutive parameters of identical primitive types whose roles differ (e.g., `(String, String)` for passenger name and seat, or user and group). Subcase B: multiple parameters of the same primitive numeric/UUID type referring to different domain ID spaces; adjacent or near-adjacent names ending in `_id` are a useful signal, but non-adjacent identifiers also qualify. Verify that the roles are semantically distinct rather than flagging every repeated type.
counterexample:
Conventional mathematical coordinates or raw matrix bounds/indices where position is standard and intuitive (e.g., `Point::new(x, y)`):
```rust
fn get_matrix_element(row: usize, col: usize) { ... }
```
A comparison function explicitly operating on two identifiers from the same ID space:
```rust
fn are_matching(id1: u64, id2: u64) -> bool { id1 == id2 }
```
Parameters already differentiated by single-variant enums or strong newtype wrappers.
source: *Mark Richards & Neal Ford - Fundamentals of Software Architecture, Chapter 3 (Modularity), Section "Connascence"*; *Implementing Domain-Driven Design* by Vaughn Vernon (p. 578); *Implementing Domain-Driven Design* by Vaughn Vernon (Chapter 10, p. 325); *Domain Modeling made Functional* (p. 83); Martin, Clean Code, p. 189 [189]; or Heather Adkins, p. 265 [374-375].
